subject: Connectivity options for private deployment: peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Carlos Mendez <carlos@edgewave.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-18T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Initial ask - secure connectivity for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Marissa,

Thanks again for the quick intro call today. EdgeWave is evaluating Redwood Private and we need guidance on what connectivity pattern makes the most sense for a constrained on-prem footprint. High-level constraints:
- 3 datacenters (two in US-West, one in US-East)
- ~1,500 inference requests/sec peak, median payload ~600 tokens (seq len ~800)
- Strict requirement: no public internet egress of customer data; encryption in transit mandatory
- Limited networking team bandwidth to manage complex BGP setups initially

Can you outline the tradeoffs between VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN for a private deployment (we may also consider Direct Connect later)? I attached a simple network diagram.

Cheers,
Carlos
Network Engineering
EdgeWave Systems

Attachments: edgewave_network_diagram.png (image)
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Initial ask - secure connectivity for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Carlos — thanks for the diagram and constraints, that helps. Looping in Karthik (solutions/network architect) and Soojin (private deployment lead).

High-level quick take so you have context while we draft a short recommendation:
- VPC peering: simplest latency-wise if you can peer customer VPCs with Redwood VPCs in the same region/account. Pros: low latency, no NAT/transit hops; Cons: peering is non-transitive (complex for multi-dc), cross-account peering requires CIDR hygiene, and peering does not natively provide granular service-level controls or per-customer endpoints.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): gives per-service endpoints hosted in your VPC and preserves IP ownership. Pros: strong isolation, easy to restrict by ENI/security groups, no need for global CIDR planning; Cons: slightly higher per-connection cost, requires NLB in front of the service, and adds an extra network hop which can slightly increase tail latency.
- Site-to-site VPN: fastest to deploy and keeps traffic over encrypted tunnels. Pros: no cloud-native changes initially, supports on-prem to Redwood Private for air-gapped-ish setups; Cons: variable performance (depends on your appliances), not ideal at scale (1,500 RPS with large tokens could tax tunnels), and operational overhead for monitoring/keepalives/BGP if you go dynamic.

Can you confirm: are you expecting symmetric egress (customer->redwood and back) for embeddings/generation? And do you need multi-dc active/active or active/passive? That will affect the recommendation.

We’ll follow up with a short decision memo and a recommended pilot path.

—Marissa
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

Thanks Carlos — below is a concise tradeoff checklist and a recommended pilot approach tailored to your traffic profile (1,500 RPS, ~800 token sequences).

Tradeoff checklist (practical bullet points):
- Latency: Peering < PrivateLink < S2S VPN (typical medians). If you need single-digit ms tail latency inside a region, peering wins.
- Scalability: PrivateLink and peering scale well; VPN appliances can be a bottleneck for sustained high throughput unless you deploy HA/clustered appliances or SD-WAN with multiple tunnels.
- Security & Audit: PrivateLink gives per-service ENI and integrates with VPC Flow Logs and security groups; peering gives full L3 access (broader blast radius unless tightly filtered); VPN provides encryption but less fine-grained cloud-side control.
- IP management: Peering requires careful CIDR non-overlap; PrivateLink preserves customer IPs behind the endpoint (NAT optional); VPN usually preserves on-prem IPs but requires route distribution.
- Operational effort: VPN fastest to get started, then PrivateLink (requires NLB + endpoint setup), peering requires networking coordination and routing updates.
- Cost: VPN has low fixed costs but performance costs if you scale appliances; PrivateLink plus NLB adds per-connection charges; peering is generally cheap except for cross-AZ/data-transfer egress.

Recommendation for pilot (2-week):
1) Phase A (rapid): Setup an S2S VPN from one US-West DC to a Redwood private environment to validate functional flow, TLS + end-to-end encryption, and SLO measurements.
2) Phase B (perf/scale): Stand up PrivateLink endpoints in a test VPC with NLBs and run a scaled traffic test (1,500 RPS synthetic) to measure tail latency and cost per token.
3) Phase C (if single-digit ms required): Evaluate VPC peering between your VPC (or colocated VPCs) and Redwood’s serving VPCs for the lowest latency path — this requires CIDR cleanup and cross-account peering approvals.

Operational notes: for the VPN phase, watch MTU (large sequences -> fragmentation), monitor VPN tunnel CPU on your appliance, and instrument flow logs on both sides to detect retransmissions. For PrivateLink, we recommend an NLB with proxy protocol and 10k rps testing to expose scale limits early.

If this approach looks reasonable, Marissa / I can draft a short mutual action plan with milestones and a list of required network artifacts (BGP config if dynamic VPN, candidate CIDRs, contact windows).

—Karthik

Carlos — thanks, all. Quick alignment and next steps below.

Decision (pilot scope):
- Start with Phase A (S2S VPN) for a 10-day smoke test to validate encryption, traffic profiles, and failure scenarios. This minimizes up-front network changes and gives you a working baseline.
- In parallel, Redwood will provision a test NLB-backed service and create PrivateLink interface endpoints for Phase B. We’ll run the 1,500 RPS synthetic workload during a scheduled window to capture p99 latency and CPU/GPU utilization.
- If Phase B shows p99 latency within your SLOs and costs are acceptable, proceed to Phase C: plan peering for the primary US-West datacenter only (reduce CIDR refactor scope).

Action items:
- EdgeWave: confirm target test CIDR(s) and provide BGP neighbor IPs if you want dynamic VPN, or device model/config if you prefer static tunnels.
- EdgeWave: provide maintenance window (2–3 hours) for the Phase B synthetic run and point-of-contact during the test.
- Redwood (Marissa/Karthik): I’ll share a one-page Mutual Action Plan and SOW draft (link below) and a short checklist for the VPN config.
